title: logPhase · The code is a byproduct
excerpt: The code is a byproduct. logPhase shows each pull request as the user journeys it changes, with the code behind every step.
content_html:
For macOS · Java · Kotlin · C# · Python · TypeScript

The code is a byproduct. The real program lives in the people who understand it.

AI now writes the code at machine speed. logPhase helps you build the understanding just as fast.

Scroll · one pull request, three user journeys

dotnet/eShop · 457 files in 6 districts · laid out by logPhase

One pull request

Watch the review in the app

You get the user journeys a pull request changes, step by step, so you understand it in minutes. All videos are real screen recordings, some sped up.

dotnet/eShop #940

How a review reads

A review starts from the blast radius of a pull request. AI writes the change. You see what it did and decide what to correct.

Every pull request opens on its journeys, then goes down to the method and the lines that changed.

  1. 01

    Paste a link

    The app clones the repository, analyses both sides of the change, and starts your Claude Code on the review.

  2. 02

    The full view first

    The change comes back as a handful of user journeys, each a flow diagram Claude writes from the code. eShop pull request #940 changed two files and touched three user journeys, and its review was finished four minutes and 20 seconds after the analysis started.

  4. 03

    The code behind a step

    Select a step and press Code to see the method behind it, the if that decides it, and the lines the pull request changed there.

    A flowchart from a chat model can't reliably show you that.

  5. 04

    What else it touches

    The call graph draws every method on the journey's path, from the analysis alone. A method's panel lists the other journeys that use it.

  6. 05

    Dig in

    Ask about any step and Claude answers from the method behind it. Split breaks a step into the smaller steps its code actually has, and Clarify asks for a plainer label. Any file opens read-only, with go to definition and a list of callers.

The code city

The Canvas draws your repository as a city at night, and lights each user journey the change touches as a trail. The layout stays put between runs, so the Ordering district is where you left it yesterday.

Why logPhase exists

In 1985, Peter Naur wrote a short essay called Programming as Theory Building. The code is not the real product of programming. The real product is the understanding the team builds: why things are the way they are, how the code maps to the business, and which changes are safe.

When the people who hold that understanding leave, the system keeps running, but nobody can change it with confidence anymore. Naur called that a dead program.

Think about the last time you inherited a service. You didn't read it top to bottom. You asked around, traced one request by hand, broke something in staging, and slowly built the theory yourself. It took weeks.

Now AI writes the code, and nobody built the theory in the first place. logPhase is how you build it, one pull request at a time.

Write to [email protected] whenever logPhase gets your repository wrong.

Try it on your next pull request.
